entries: On the eighth day after His birth, in keeping with the Law of Moses, the Child was circumcised and given the name Jesus, the name the angel had announced before He was conceived (Luke 2:21). The Church sees in this feast the Lord’s willing submission to the Law He came to fulfil, and keeps it as the eighth day of the Nativity and the first day of the civil year.

St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379), Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, was a theologian, monastic legislator and defender of the Nicene faith whose Liturgy is still used in the Church. His friend St. Gregory of Nazianzus, called the Theologian (c. 329–390), briefly served as Archbishop of Constantinople and left orations and poems of lasting authority on the Holy Trinity. The Church remembers them together with all the holy Fathers who guarded the apostolic faith. Basil reposed on 1 January 379.

The Church greets the first day of the civil year with prayer and thanksgiving, giving thanks to God for the mercies of the year that has passed and committing the year to come to His keeping. The faithful ask the Lord’s blessing on their homes, their work and their nation, and pray that the new year may be lived in peace, in faith and in the service of others.

Born on 16 June 1874 at Kurichy, Kottayam, into the Kallacheril family, Punnoose was ordained priest in 1898 and consecrated Metropolitan Geevarghese Mar Gregorios by Patriarch Abded Mshiho II on 8 September 1912. Enthroned Catholicos of the East on 15 February 1929 and chosen Malankara Metropolitan in 1934, he raised the Catholicate headquarters at Devalokam and declared St. Gregorios of Parumala and St. Basil Yeldho saints in 1947. He reposed on 3 January 1964, aged 89, and rests beside the Devalokam Aramana chapel.

On this day the Church remembers the Oath taken in 1653 at Mattancherry, when thousands of Malankara Christians, grieved by the seizure of the prelate Ahatallah, gathered at the ancient stone cross, held its ropes and vowed never to submit to Portuguese rule over their Church. Known as the Coonan Cross Oath, it is the foundation of the Church’s later independence, and its memorial is kept at St. George Orthodox Church, Mattancherry.

The Second Sunday after Christmas continues the Church’s rejoicing in the birth of Christ, before the season turns to His manifestation at the Jordan. The faithful are called to live in the light of the Incarnation, confessing with the Gospel of John that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and to carry the joy of the Nativity into the new year.

Epiphany, called Denho, celebrates the baptism of Jesus Christ in the Jordan by John the Baptist, when the heavens were opened, the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father’s voice declared Him the beloved Son (Matthew 3:13–17). The Church sees in it the manifestation of the Holy Trinity and the sanctifying of the waters, and blesses water on this day as a sign of the new creation.

The son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, John lived in the wilderness until he began to preach repentance beside the Jordan. He baptised Jesus Christ and pointed to Him as the Lamb of God, and the Church keeps this commemoration on the day after the Feast of Denho. Sent as the Forerunner to prepare the way of the Lord, he was later imprisoned and beheaded by Herod Antipas.

One of the seven deacons chosen by the apostles at Jerusalem, Stephen was full of faith and the Holy Spirit and worked great signs among the people. Accused of blasphemy before the council, he bore witness from the Scriptures and was stoned outside the city, praying for his killers while the young Saul looked on. Venerated as the Archdeacon and first martyr of the Church, he is remembered with great honour.

The Sundays after Epiphany celebrate the manifestation of Christ to the world, and the first of them invites the faithful to contemplate the Lord’s baptism and to renew their own. Sealed with the Holy Spirit at baptism, they are called to live as children of the light, to follow the Lord who was revealed at the Jordan, and to make Him known to others.

On 15 January the Church keeps the Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary for the Seeds, asking the prayers of the Mother of God for the sowing of the fields and for the fruitfulness of the earth. The faithful give thanks to God who gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater, and entrust to Him the labour of the land and the year’s harvest.

Born in the Egyptian Thebaid about 227 to a wealthy Christian family, Paul fled the persecution of Decius and found refuge in a desert cave, where he lived in prayer for nearly ninety years, nourished, according to tradition, by a palm tree and bread brought by a raven. He is remembered as the first Christian hermit. In his old age St. Antony visited him and, after his repose about 342, buried him.

Sent from Antioch at the repeated requests of Archdeacon Thoma, the prelate Ahatallah reached the coast of India in the early 1650s but was seized by the Portuguese and held at Mylapore. Taken by ship towards Goa, he was stopped at Cochin, where thousands of Syrian Christians gathered to demand his release, and was reportedly drowned there that night. The Coonan Cross Oath of 1653 followed, and he is remembered as a martyr of the Malankara Church.

The Synod of Mavelikkara met at St. Mary’s Church, Puthiyakavu, on 16 January 1836 under Cheppad Philipose Mar Dionysius, with the clergy and lay leaders of the Malankara Church. Its Padiyola resisted the reforms urged by the CMS missionaries and reaffirmed the Church’s ancient faith, order and independence, and the synod is remembered as a landmark in the Church’s history in the nineteenth century.

The Second Sunday after Epiphany continues the season of the Lord’s manifestation, when the Church remembers how Christ, revealed at the Jordan, began His ministry among the people. The faithful are invited to listen to His word, to follow Him as the first disciples did, and to bear witness to the light that was shown at His baptism.

St. Samuel of Qartmin, son of the wealthy Yuhannon of Eshtin near Sawro in Tur Abdin, lived in the early fifth century, and his prayers healed the child Simeon, who grew up as his disciple and a monk of Qartmin. St. Antony, born about 251 CE at Koma in Upper Egypt to a wealthy Christian family, gave away his inheritance and withdrew into the desert, where his life of prayer drew many disciples and made him the father of monasticism. He reposed in 356 CE, aged 105.

Born on 16 June 1931 at Naranganam, Kozhencherry, the fourth son of P. G. Thomas, Philipose worked in the Indian Railways from 1954 to 1962 before studying theology at Serampore and Geneva. Ordained priest in 1974 and made Ramban in 1983, he was consecrated Philipose Mar Eusebios on 15 May 1985 and took full charge of the Thumpamon Diocese in 1990. A theologian and ecumenical representative, he reposed on 21 January 2009 and rests at St. Basil Aramana Chapel, Pathanamthitta.

Born in Egypt in the time of Constantine, Mar Augen was a pearl-fisher at Clysma on the Red Sea who shared his catch with the poor for some twenty-five years before becoming a monk under St. Pachomius. He then went to Mesopotamia, settled on Mount Izla near Nisibis and founded many monasteries, and is revered as the father of Syrian monasticism. He is honoured in all the Churches of the Syriac tradition, and his feast is kept on 23 January.

Pethurtho, the Sunday before the Nineveh Lent, prepares the faithful for the Three-Day Lent of Nineveh, recalling how the people of that city repented at the preaching of the prophet Jonah and were spared. Before the fast begins, the Church prays for a heart of repentance and for God’s mercy on His people, and invites the faithful to enter the fast with prayer and almsgiving.

The Church remembers all the departed Fathers and Malpans, the bishops, priests, teachers and scholars who handed on the faith, the Scriptures and the liturgy of the Church, and prays for their repose. The faithful give thanks for those who taught them the way of Christ, and ask that they may be gathered with the saints in the Kingdom of God.

Born in 1869 at Angamaly, Paulose studied at Aluva and Kottayam and was invited to Thrikkunnath by Kadavil Mar Athanasius to supervise the building of St. Mary’s Church. Raised to Ramban by Mar Gregorios of Parumala, he became known as Kochu Paulose Ramban and served as Metropolitan, remembered as the Valiya Thirumeni of Aluva. He took part in the 1911 Holy Chrism consecration at Mulanthuruthy and reposed on 25 January 1953.

On this Monday the Three-Day Lent of Nineveh begins, a fast of three days kept by the Syriac Churches in memory of the repentance of Nineveh at the preaching of the prophet Jonah (Jonah 3). The faithful fast and pray for the forgiveness of sins and for God’s mercy on His people, trusting that He who spared the repentant city will hear those who turn to Him.

Born on 30 January 1915 at Perinad, Kollam, he was ordained deacon in 1938 and priest in 1941, and consecrated Episcopa as Mathews Mar Coorilos on 15 May 1953. Elected successor to the Catholicate in 1980, he became sixth Catholicos of the East and Malankara Metropolitan in 1991 and was loved as “Angel Bava” for his gentleness. An orator and theologian, he reposed on 26 January 2006 and rests at Mount Horeb, Shasthamkotta.

Pakalomattom Thoma Kathanar was consecrated Mar Thoma VIII at Kandanad in July 1809 by the dying Mar Thoma VII and was acclaimed Malankara Metropolitan that September. He backed Pulikkottil Ittoop Ramban in laying the foundation stone of the Kottayam Syrian Seminary in February 1813, which brought modern education to Kerala. He consecrated his uncle Kadamattathu Iype Kathanar as Mar Thoma IX, reposed on 26 January 1816 and rests at St. Mary’s Cathedral, Puthenkavu.

On 26 January 1950 the Constitution of India came into force and the country became a sovereign democratic republic. The Church gives thanks for the freedom and constitutional order of the nation, and prays for its leaders and people, that justice, peace and the common good may prevail among all its communities.

The Three-Day Lent of Nineveh ends with the Holy Qurbana, and the faithful break their fast with thanksgiving to God, who spared the people of Nineveh when they turned from their evil ways. The Church remembers the prophet Jonah and gives thanks for the mercy of God, who desires not the death of the sinner but that he should turn and live.

The Prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, was sent by God to preach repentance to the great city of Nineveh. He fled by sea, was thrown overboard in a storm and spent three days in the belly of a great fish before being cast ashore, a sign the Church sees as foreshadowing Christ’s burial and resurrection. His preaching moved Nineveh to fast and repent, and this repentance is remembered each year in the Three-Day Lent of Nineveh.

Born c. 465 at Sozopolis in Pisidia into a wealthy family, Severios studied at Alexandria, took monastic vows at a Gaza monastery and was ordained priest. Enthroned Patriarch of Antioch on 6 November 512, he lived as a monk and defended the one nature of Christ in treatises, hymns and liturgical prayers. Exiled in 518, he spent twenty years in hiding and reposed in Egypt on 8 February 538, aged 79.

On this Sunday the Church remembers all the priests who have fallen asleep in the Lord, praying for the repose of those who served at the altar, preached the Gospel and shepherded the faithful. The people give thanks for their ministry of the sacraments and ask God to forgive their failings and to receive them among the saints who served Him.

Mayaltho commemorates the forty-day-old Christ being brought by Mary and Joseph to the Temple at Jerusalem, in obedience to the Law, with the offering of a pair of turtledoves. Simeon and Anna recognised Him as the salvation promised to Israel (Luke 2:22–38). The Church sees in the feast the meeting of the Lord with His people and gives thanks for His coming in the flesh.

St. Simeon, a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem, had been promised by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. When the infant Jesus was presented in the Temple he took Him in his arms and gave thanks, and the aged prophetess Anna, who served in the Temple with fasting and prayer, spoke of the child to all who awaited redemption. The Church honours them as the Elders of the Presentation.

Born in 1886 at Tripunithura, M. P. Peter taught in schools, took part in the Vaikom satyagraha and gave up teaching for missionary work. Ordained deacon in 1916 and priest in 1926, he founded the Servants of the Cross Society in 1924 to uplift Dalit Christians. Consecrated Metropolitan of Malabar in 1953, he is remembered as the “Malankara Gandhi”. He reposed on 2 February 1968 and rests at Carmel Dayara, Kandanad.

St. Barsauma, the Chief of Mourners, was a fifth-century Syrian monk and archimandrite who gathered monks around him in the mountains near Melitene and became a spiritual father to the monks of the East. He took part in the Council of Ephesus in 449 and reposed about 458, and the monastery that bears his name later served the Patriarchs of Antioch. St. Kauma, known as Shemvun Qaumo the Mourner, was a fifth-century saint who prayed standing for forty-five years in the shape of a cross.

Born into the Kidangan family of Kunnamkulam, Geevarghese served as vicar of Arthat Church before being consecrated Metropolitan Philoxenos for Thozhiyur about 1812. Acting as Malankara Metropolitan from 1816 and managing the Church’s Vattipanam fund, he consecrated three Malankara Metropolitans in turn: Pulikkottil Joseph Mar Dionysius II on 21 March 1815, Punnathra Mar Dionysius III in 1817 and Cheppad Philipose Mar Dionysius IV on 27 August 1825. He reposed on 7 February 1829 and was buried at St. George’s Church, Thozhiyur.

On the Sunday before the Great Lent the Church remembers all the faithful departed, praying that God may forgive their sins and give them rest with the righteous. The people recall that this life is a journey toward the Kingdom, and that the living and the departed are one communion in Christ, awaiting the day of resurrection.

A holy man from Nineveh in present-day Iraq, Mar Abo reached Kollam on foot, perhaps to venerate the tomb of St. Thomas or to escape persecution in Persia. He preached at Kadamattom, Akaparambu, Kayamkulam, Niranam and Thevalakkara, helped establish churches, and healed the sick of every caste. His disciple was Kadamattom Kathanar. He reposed at Thevalakkara, where his tomb lies in St. Mary’s Church and his feast is kept each February.

Born in 1928 at Chenkulam near Kollam, Mathews studied physics and education and taught in schools before following Metropolitan Mathews Mar Coorilos into the ministry. Ordained priest in 1958, he served Kollam parishes, became a Ramban in 1983 and was consecrated Episcopa in 1985. Elevated Metropolitan of Kollam in 1991, he was loved as “Sowmya Thejas of Malankara”. He reposed on 9 February 2009 and rests at St. Thomas Cathedral, Kollam.

Born Nasri in 1867 at Mardin, the second son of Corepiscopus Abraham, he joined Deyrul Zafaran, was ordained deacon in 1887, monk in 1889 and priest in 1892, and sheltered thousands of Armenian refugees. Consecrated Bishop of Amid in 1908 and Patriarch of Antioch in 1917, he travelled to India in 1931 at the Viceroy’s request to seek peace in the Church. He reposed on 13 February 1932 at Manjinikkara and is entombed there at Mor Ignatios Dayro.

The first Sunday of the Great Lent recalls the wedding at Cana in Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine as the first of His signs (John 2:1–11), and sets the tone of the fast by calling the faithful to look back on their lives and to bring their poverty to the Lord. The fifty days of the Great Lent begin with the service of mutual forgiveness.

Born on 11 August 1951 at Ramamangalam, Muvattupuzha, the youngest of seven children of Kuriako and Annamma, Kuriako Yohannan, called Onankunju, studied up to the seventh class at Ooramana Government High School and, unmarried, devoted himself zealously to the Church. On 15 February 1976, returning in a lorry from the welcome given to Catholicos Mathews I at Ernakulam, he was struck on the head by a brick thrown at the vehicle and died, aged twenty-four, a martyr for the Church. He rests at St. George’s Church, Kadamattom.

Shubqono, “forgiveness”, is the service of mutual pardon with which the Great Lent begins: the faithful ask and give forgiveness to one another and to God, in obedience to the Lord’s teaching that those who forgive others will be forgiven (Matthew 6:14). Reconciled with their neighbours, they enter the fifty days of fasting, prayer and almsgiving that lead to the Resurrection.

Born at Mavelikkara, Geevarghese became a theologian, orator and writer, widely known as a prophet of social justice and an apostle of sharing. Ordained priest in 1956, he was consecrated bishop by Baselios Augen I at Niranam in 1975 and served as Metropolitan of Niranam until 2007. He led the Church’s Mission Board and was honoured by the Church with the title Sabharathnam. He reposed on 16 February 2012, aged 94.

St. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and Edessa, taught the faith in verse and hymn and is called the Harp of the Holy Spirit. St. Theodore, a young soldier martyred under Maximian about 306, is remembered on the first Saturday of Great Lent because he appeared in 361 to warn the archbishop of Constantinople that the food in the markets had been defiled on Julian’s orders, so that the faithful ate boiled wheat instead.

Mar Danaha was a prelate who came to Malankara in 905 CE with three monks, Rabban Ramban, Yaunan Ramban and Avan, who is thought to be Mar Abo. They were sent from the East by Mor Athanasius, the Maphrian, who had been consecrated that year by Patriarch Dionysius II of Antioch. Mar Danaha reposed at Kudassanad while staying at the house of Kannom Mappila of the Valiyaveedu family and was buried near that house, where he is remembered at the Valiyaveettil Mar Danaha family chapel.

Leper’s Sunday recalls the leper who came to Jesus and said, “Lord, if You will, You can make me clean”, and was healed by the Lord’s touch (Matthew 8:1–4). The Church prays for healing from the leprosy of sin and finds in the Lord’s word the pardon He gives to the repentant, who are then sent to show themselves and to give thanks.

Five members of a Brahmin family of North Paravur, four men and a woman, became Christians and were cast out of their community. They came to Pandalam, where the king took pity and let them settle at Thalayanad. The eldest, a yogi, healed the sick by his prayers and was called Thalayanad Appooppan. Buried there with the others, he went on giving relief to those who prayed at his grave, and eight and a half Christian families of the neighbouring parish built a church and keep a yearly festival in his name.

Bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostle John, Polycarp linked the apostles to the later Church and taught St. Irenaeus. When the proconsul urged him to curse Christ, he answered that he had served the Lord eighty-six years and had received no wrong from Him. He was burned and then pierced with a sword at Smyrna about 155 CE, and is revered as a martyr and one of the Apostolic Fathers.

Born on 31 October 1858 at Mallappally into the Vattasseril family, Geevarghese served as Malpan of the Old Seminary, Kottayam, and was consecrated Metropolitan Dionysius at Mosul on 31 May 1908. Malankara Metropolitan from 1909, he led the Church in its struggle for independence, took part in re-establishing the Catholicate in 1912 and is remembered as the Illuminator. He reposed on 23 February 1934 and rests at the Old Seminary Chapel, Kottayam; the Church declared him a saint in February 2003.

Born on 26 May 1926 at Ayroor to Chacko and Mariamma Kuttikandathil, Thomas was ordained priest at St. Thomas Cathedral, Madras, in September 1952 and taught Church History at the Orthodox Theological Seminary, Kottayam. Consecrated Metropolitan by Catholicos Augen I in 1975, he was first Metropolitan of Bombay, of the American Diocese from 1979 and of the Canada, UK and Europe Diocese from 1994. He reposed on 23 February 2008, after a car accident in Britain, and rests at the Catholicate Palace, Devalokam.

A tax collector at Capernaum, Matthew left his customs booth at the call of Jesus and became one of the Twelve, giving a feast for the Lord with his fellow publicans. The first Gospel is ascribed to him, written chiefly for Jewish readers to show Jesus as the promised Messiah. According to Church tradition he preached in Judea and then in distant lands, and ended his life as a martyr.

Palsy Sunday recalls the paralysed man whom his friends lowered through the roof to Jesus, who said to him, “Your sins are forgiven; rise and walk” (Mark 2:1–12). It teaches that the Lord heals soul and body alike, and that faith and the help of friends bring the sick to Him. The faithful pray for forgiveness and for strength to rise and walk in His way.

A prelate from Tur Abdin known as Kallada Valiyappoopan, Mar Anthrayos came to Kerala in 1678 with three brothers, one of them a Ramban, and lived for many years at Mulanthuruthy. He gave away his wealth to the poor and travelled through Piravom, Manarcad and Puthenkavu to Kallada; his wooden horse is still preserved at Puthenkavu. He reposed on 2 March 1692 and is entombed beneath the altar of Kallada Church, now a pilgrim centre.

A Syriac scholar of the Konat family of Pampakuda and a Malankara Malpan, Abraham was elected Priest Trustee of the Church in 1982 on the proposal of Baselios Marthoma Mathews I. He also served for many years as president of the Pampakuda Panchayat, caring for the people of his village as well as the Church. He reposed on 2 March 1987 and was buried at Pampakuda.

This Sunday recalls the woman of Tyre and Sidon who pleaded with the Lord to heal her daughter and was answered, “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matthew 15:21–28). The Church holds up her persistence and humility as a model of prayer, and sees in her the coming of the nations to Christ, who has mercy on all who call upon Him in faith.

Forty soldiers of the Roman army stationed at Sebaste in Armenia refused to deny Christ under the emperor Licinius about 320 CE. They were stripped and left to stand all night on a frozen lake, with a warm bath on the shore to tempt them; one man left, but a guard who watched them confessed Christ and took his place. At dawn the martyrs’ bodies were burned, and the Church honours them as models of steadfastness.

Born about 1834 as the third son of Ittimathu and Elikutty of the Ambatt Vadakkan family of Akaparambu, Geevarghese was ordained deacon by Yuyakkim Mar Koorilos and served as priest in his home parish, the Mar Sabor-Mar Aphroth Church. Raised Ramban by Patriarch Peter III, he was consecrated Mar Coorilos Geevarghese at North Paravur on 10 December 1876 and given the Angamaly diocese. He reposed on 9 March 1891, aged 56, and was interred in the tomb he had prepared.

A Syriac scholar of the priestly Konat family of Pampakuda, Yuhanon taught the clergy of the Church and was a teacher of his kinsman Konat Geevarghese Mar Julius. Elected Priest Trustee at the Association meeting of 11–13 September 1886, he served the Church as Malankara Malpan until his death on 9 March 1890. His son Konat Mathen Malpan succeeded him as Priest Trustee.

Mid-Lent marks the middle of the Great Lent, when the Church pauses to encourage the faithful who have laboured in the fast and to strengthen them to complete it. The day is kept with special prayers, and the Church also remembers King Abgar of Edessa, whose faith in the Lord brought the Gospel to his city.

Abgar V, called Ukkama, ruled Edessa (Urhai) and Osroene in the first century. Tradition tells that he wrote to Jesus asking for healing and received a reply, and that after the Ascension he was healed and baptised by Addai, one of the Seventy, who preached in the city. Edessa thus became an early centre of Syriac Christianity, and the Church remembers Abgar as its first Christian king.

This Sunday recalls the woman bent double for eighteen years whom Jesus healed on the Sabbath, laying His hands on her and saying, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity” (Luke 13:10–17). The faithful pray to be freed from whatever bows them down, and to stand upright in praise of God, who raises up those who are bowed down.

Born in 1910 at Cherai, Paulose Mulayirikkal was ordained deacon in 1926 and priest in 1930 by Mar Athanasius Paulose, whose Thrikkunnath Seminary he joined. Made a Ramban in 1934, he was consecrated by Patriarch Ignatius Aphrem I as Mar Severios and revived a diocese that had no assets of its own. He reposed suddenly on 17 March 1962 at Kunnamkulam, while preparing to lead the feast of Mar Osthathios Sleeba.

Born in 1854 at Kafarso near Amid in south-east Turkey, Sleeba studied Syriac and theology and came to Malankara as a deacon in 1881 with Mar Athanasius Shem’vun. Consecrated Bishop Osthathios Sleeba at Mosul in 1908, he returned with Mar Dionysius Vattasseril. Living in simplicity, prayer and fasting, he pioneered the Sunday School movement and established and consecrated many parishes. He reposed on 19 March 1930 and rests at Arthat, Kunnamkulam.

This Sunday recalls the man born blind whom Jesus healed by anointing his eyes with clay and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam, so that he saw and confessed his faith (John 9). The Church sees in the story the enlightenment of baptism, and prays that those once blind in sin may see the Light of the world.

Thomas of Cana, a merchant of Syrian Christian descent, is remembered by the tradition of Malankara as the leader of the Christian families who came from Mesopotamia and Persia to Kodungallur (Cranganore) about 345 CE, accompanied by Bishop Mar Joseph of Edessa, priests and deacons. Welcomed by the ruler Cheraman Perumal, the company received lands and privileges inscribed on copper plates, and strengthened the Christian community of Malabar.

Catholicate Day is kept on the sixth Sunday of the Great Lent in honour of the Catholicate of the East, the apostolic throne of St. Thomas, which was re-established in Malankara in 1912. The faithful pray for the Catholicos and the Church, give thanks for its independence and for the leaders who served it, and make their offering for the support of the Catholicate.

Suboro commemorates the archangel Gabriel’s announcement to the Virgin Mary at Nazareth that she would conceive and bear the Son of the Most High, and her reply, “Let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:26–38). The Church honours the moment of the Incarnation and the obedience of the Mother of God, and the feast falls nine months before Christmas.

A Vedic Brahmin of the Pakalomattom family baptised by St. Thomas in 52 CE, Valiya Auppan, the chief priest, preached the Gospel from Kuravilangad toward Niranam, the church founded by his guru. Resting at Muthavazhi near Chengannur, he prayed in the name of Jesus for the childless head of the Chithrathoor Brahmin Madom, and a son was born within the year. The madom gave him half its property, where, a celibate priest, he settled with his younger brother’s family; the cleared land gave the Kaduvettoor family its name.

Of the Pakalomattom family, Mar Thoma IV was chosen by the Church’s leaders after the sudden death of Mar Thoma III and consecrated in 1688 by Mar Ivanios Hidayatullah. He guided the Malankara Church for four decades through persecutions and the rival claims of the East Syrian bishop Mar Gabriel. He had Mar Thoma V consecrated as his successor, reposed on 24 March 1728 and rests at Marth Mariam Church, Kandanad.

The fortieth day of the Great Lent marks the completion of the forty days of fasting, recalling the Lord’s forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–2), before the Church turns to Lazarus Saturday, Palm Sunday and the Passion Week. The faithful, who have fasted and prayed through the Lent, are called to prepare their hearts to follow the Lord to Jerusalem and to the Cross.

The Saturday before Palm Sunday recalls the raising of Lazarus of Bethany, four days dead, whom the Lord called from the tomb (John 11:1–44), a sign of His own coming resurrection and of the general resurrection of the dead. The Church keeps the day as the gateway to the Passion Week and praises Christ, the Resurrection and the Life.

Palm Sunday recalls the Lord’s entry into Jerusalem on a donkey, welcomed by crowds who spread their garments and palm branches on the road and cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew 21:1–17). The children’s praise in the Temple is remembered, and the Church keeps the day as Boys’ and Girls’ Day, carrying palm leaves in procession and greeting Christ as King.

Born in 1829 into the priestly Konat family of Pampakuda, Geevarghese studied under his relatives Konat Abraham and Konat Yuhanon Malpan and became a Syriac scholar whose pupils included Gregorios of Parumala. Raised Ramban by Patriarch Peter III in 1875, he was consecrated Metropolitan Julius at North Paravur on 3 December 1876 as first bishop of the new Thumpamon diocese. He founded the Kerala Deepam Press at Pampakuda in 1879 and is entombed in the Konat family chapel at St. John’s Ephesus Church there.

Holy Monday opens the days of the Passion Week, which the Church spends in prayer, fasting and the reading of the Lord’s last days in Jerusalem. The day recalls the cursing of the barren fig tree (Matthew 21:18–22), a warning against faith that bears no fruit, and calls the faithful to repentance as they follow the Lord toward the Cross.

On Holy Tuesday the Church remembers the Lord’s teaching in the Temple in His last days, His answers to the authorities and His parables of watchfulness, among them the ten virgins and the talents (Matthew 24–25). The faithful are urged to keep their lamps burning and to be ready for the coming of the Bridegroom.

Born at Peringara near Thiruvalla as the only son of Varkey Asan of the Panickerveettil family, Varkey Varghese was a teacher and a wrestler of giant build, which earned him the name Anapapy. Sent from Thiruvalla by the Church’s leaders, he became chief of the bodyguards of St. Dionysius of Vattasseril at the Old Seminary, Kottayam. On 31 March 1912, aged about thirty-five, he was attacked by a gang on the bank of the Meenachil and died of his wounds, a martyr. He rests at Kottayam Mar Barsauma Orthodox Church.

Holy Wednesday recalls the woman who anointed the Lord at Bethany with costly ointment (Mark 14:3–9), and Judas Iscariot’s bargain to betray his Master for thirty pieces of silver. The Church sets the woman’s love against the traitor’s greed as it draws near the Passion, and prays to be kept faithful to the Lord to the end.

A celibate and ascetic priest, Geevarghese Kathanar served as one of the vicars of St. Mary’s Church, Chengannur, and later moved to Perissery, which then lay under a different fief, where he built a church. Revered by the faithful as Palliyil Appooppan, the venerable elder of the Church, he was buried at St. Mary’s Church, Perissery, Chengannur, where his memory is kept.

On Passover Thursday the Church remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus washed the disciples’ feet, gave His Body and Blood in the bread and the cup and bade them do this in His memory (John 13; Luke 22). The service includes the washing of feet and the Holy Qurbana of the Institution, and in Kerala the faithful share the unleavened Pesaha bread in their homes that night.

Good Friday commemorates the Lord’s trial, scourging, crucifixion and death on Golgotha. The Church keeps a day of strict fasting and prayer without the Holy Qurbana, with long readings of the Passion, the veneration of the Cross and the burial service, and the faithful break their fast with plain gruel. The Cross, the instrument of shame, is honoured as the sign of salvation.

Gospel Saturday, the Saturday of Good Tidings, remembers the Lord’s rest in the tomb and His descent to the dead to proclaim salvation to the righteous of old. The Church keeps vigil in expectation, reading of the burial (Matthew 27:57–66), and prepares to proclaim the good news of the Resurrection that is to be heard on Easter morning.

Easter, Qyamtho, is the feast of feasts, when the Church celebrates the Resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day after His crucifixion, the victory over sin and death on which the whole faith rests (1 Corinthians 15). The faithful greet one another with the joyful news that Christ is risen, and keep fifty days of rejoicing until Pentecost.

Born on 5 April 1885 at Pezhamattam, Pampady, Kuriakose was ordained sub-deacon at fourteen, studied under Vattasseril Geevarghese Malpan at the Old Seminary and was made priest and Ramban on 8 and 9 July 1906. From 1914 he lived as a hermit on the Pothenpuram hills, where Mount Tabor Dayara arose, and on 16 February 1929 became the first Metropolitan consecrated by a Catholicos. Revered for prayer and charity to the poor, he reposed on 5 April 1965 and rests at Mount Tabor Dayara, now renamed St. Kuriakose Dayara.

On Bright Monday the Church, which keeps the whole week after Easter as one joyful day, pauses at the empty tomb and rejoices with the women who found the stone rolled away and heard the angel announce that the Lord had risen. There is no fasting in the Bright Week, and the faithful greet one another with the good news of the Resurrection.

On Bright Tuesday the Church remembers how the risen Lord appeared to Mary Magdalene in the garden and sent her to tell the disciples that He was alive (John 20:11–18). The faithful are reminded that the first witness of the Resurrection was a woman who loved Him, and are called to carry the same news to others.

On Bright Wednesday the Church recalls the risen Lord walking with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, opening the Scriptures to them and making Himself known in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:13–35). The day is a feast of the Word and of the Eucharist, in which the faithful too meet the living Christ.

On Bright Thursday the Church remembers the Lord’s appearance to His disciples gathered behind locked doors, when He showed them His hands and His side and gave them His peace (John 20:19–23). The faithful receive the same peace from the risen Lord and are sent, as the disciples were, to proclaim the forgiveness of sins.

Born Iype, the only son of Mathen Tharakan of the Pakalomattom family at Thazhamon, Ayroor, he succeeded Mar Thoma V and was ordained Metropolitan on 8 May 1765. Consecrated by an Antiochene bishop, he was the first Malankara father to take the name Dionysius and is remembered as Valiya Mar Dionysius. His long reign passed through persecutions and Tipu Sultan’s invasion; he reposed on 8 April 1808 and was interred at St. Mary’s Church, Puthencavu.

Bright Friday continues the week of Easter joy, in which the Church sings the victory of the Cross and the Resurrection together. On this day the Church also keeps the Commemoration of the Confessors, and the faithful give thanks that Christ, who rose from the dead, gives strength to those who bear witness to Him.

On this Friday of the Bright Week the Church commemorates the confessors, those who suffered imprisonment, torture and exile for their faith in Christ without being put to death, and who held fast to the faith under persecution. They are honoured with the martyrs, and the faithful ask their prayers and give thanks for their steadfast witness.

Bright Saturday brings the week of Easter to its close, with thanksgiving for the Resurrection and with the Church’s eyes already turned to New Sunday, when the Lord appeared to Thomas. The faithful have been fed for a week with the good news of the Resurrection and are sent back to ordinary life to live it.

New Sunday, the Sunday after Easter, recalls the Lord’s appearance to His disciples a week after the Resurrection, when Thomas, who had doubted, put his hand into His side and confessed, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:24–29). The Church of India reveres Thomas as its apostle and keeps the day with special joy.

Born on 14 November 1940 at Madurai into the Keeyath family of Protestants, the third son of K. George and Annamma, he studied in England as a deacon, was ordained priest in 1973 and taught at the Orthodox Theological Seminary. Consecrated Geevarghese Mar Ivanios at Puthenkavu on 15 May 1985, he served as Metropolitan of Kottayam and was honoured as a man of unceasing prayer. He reposed on 12 April 2013 and rests at Mar Baselios Dayara, Kottayam.

Born into the Parampil house of the Pakalomattom family at Kuravilangad, the nephew of Mar Thoma I was consecrated in 1670 by his uncle and Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel of Jerusalem. By his time the Church had adopted Syriac usages such as the western calendar, baptismal fonts and pulpits. Struck by lightning while resting at St. Mary’s Church, Niranam, he reposed in April 1686 and rests there, where a side altar serves as his shrine.

Born on 10 June 1897 into the Kizhekethalackal family of Puthenkavu, Chengannur, the third son of Thomas Kathanar, he took an M.A. in English at Calcutta and was ordained deacon and priest in 1929. Consecrated Metropolitan of Thumpamon at Parumala on 3 November 1930, he was called Kochu Thirumeni as the youngest Metropolitan and founded many schools in mid-Travancore. He died of a heart attack on 17 April 1951, aged 53, and rests at St. Mary’s Cathedral, Puthenkavu.

The second Sunday after Easter is the first of the Sundays that follow New Sunday in the fifty days of Easter joy. In these weeks the Church dwells on the risen Lord’s appearances and teaching, and strengthens the faithful in the hope of the resurrection and in the life of the Spirit that He promised His disciples.

Born at Mosul, Yuhanon was made Ramban at Deyrul Zafaran and ordained priest in 1724. Sent to Malankara with Maphrian Baselios Shukrallah, he was consecrated bishop as Mar Ivanios Yuhanon at Kandanad in 1752 and, with Mar Gregorios Yuhanon, consecrated Mar Thoma VI in 1770, then laboured for peace in the Church until his death. He reposed in April 1794 and is entombed at the Old Syrian Church, Chengannur.

Of the Pakalomattom family of Kadamattom, he was chosen after the sudden death of Mar Thoma II and consecrated in 1686 by Mar Ivanios Hidayatullah, then the only bishop in Malankara. He strove to visit as many parishes as possible. He died suddenly at Kadampanad in April 1688 and was laid to rest on 22 April in the sanctuary of St. Thomas Valiyapally, now the Orthodox Cathedral.

A soldier of Cappadocian origin in the Roman army, George confessed Christ before the emperor Diocletian and endured torture and death at Lydda in Palestine about 303 CE. His courage made him one of the best loved martyrs of the whole Church, venerated in the Syriac tradition as Mor Geevarghese Sahada. Many churches of Malankara bear his name, and his relics rest at Lydda.

John Mark, the companion of Barnabas and Paul and later of Peter, is the traditional author of the Second Gospel, which preserves the apostle Peter’s preaching. Tradition holds that he founded the Church of Alexandria and was its first bishop, and that he was dragged through the streets by a mob and martyred about 68 CE. His mother’s house in Jerusalem was an early gathering place of the disciples.

Archdeacon Thomas of the Parampil house of the Pakalomattom family at Kuravilangad led the Church after the Coonan Cross Oath of January 1653, and later that year twelve priests laid hands on him at Alangad and he became Mar Thoma I, the first native Metropolitan of Malankara. His episcopate was confirmed in 1665 by Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel of Jerusalem, and he guided the Church through years of persecution. He reposed on 25 April 1670 and was interred at Marth Mariam Church, Angamaly.

The third Sunday after Easter continues the season of the Resurrection, in which the Church sings of the Lord who has trampled down death. The faithful are called to live as people of the resurrection, to share the good news with others and to keep the joy of Easter in their lives beyond the Bright Week.

Born at Mosul, Abdul Jaleel was ordained priest, then bishop for Amid in 1654, and later Metropolitan of Jerusalem with the name Gregorios. Sent to the troubled Malankara Church, he landed on the Kerala coast in 1664, consecrated Archdeacon Thoma as Mar Thoma I on 1 July 1665 and with him consecrated Mar Thoma II, restoring Syriac usages in the parishes. He reposed on 27 April 1671 and is entombed at St. Thomas Church, North Paravur.

Mar Sabor and Mar Afroth, two holy brother bishops and monks from Persia, came to Kerala as missionaries with a company of settlers led by the merchant Marvan Sapor Esho, landing at Kollam in 823 CE according to tradition. Welcomed by the Chera ruler Iyyanadikal Thiruvadikal, they built churches in the Syriac tradition, called the Kadeeshangal, and the Tharisapally copper plates record the grant for the church at Kollam. Both are believed to have died in Kerala, and the ancient church at Akaparambu bears their names.

James, the elder son of Zebedee and brother of the apostle John, was among the first disciples called by the Lord beside the Sea of Galilee. With Peter and John he witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane, and was called a Son of Thunder for his zeal. He was beheaded by Herod Agrippa I about 44 CE, the first of the apostles to die as a martyr.

Born on 19 January 1836 at Vettithara near Kolenchery, he was ordained deacon by Cheppad Mar Dionysius in 1843 and priest in 1852, and long served as vicar of Kolenchery. Consecrated Metropolitan Paulose Mar Ivanios of Kandanad by Patriarch Peter III at Kunnamkulam on 17 May 1877, he was enthroned the first Catholicos of the East at Niranam on 15 September 1912. He founded the Malankara Suriyani Suvishesha Sangham, reposed on 2 May 1913 and rests at Pampakuda Cheriyapally.

Born on 24 February 1927 at Kallada, C. I. Geevarghese Ramban was a member of the Order of the Sacred Transfiguration of Mount Tabor Dayara, Pathanapuram. He founded the St. George Ashram at Kulamudy, where he lived the monastic life of prayer and simplicity, and the Church remembers him among the ascetics of the Order who gave themselves wholly to God.

The fourth Sunday after Easter continues the fifty days between the Resurrection and Pentecost. The Church, which has listened to the accounts of the risen Lord, prays that the faithful may know Him in the Scriptures and in the breaking of the bread, and may walk in the newness of life given in baptism.

Born in 1916 at Vennikkulam, C. P. Chandy served the Church’s Balasamajam, Sunday School, Students’ and Youth movements before dedicating his life to it from 1940, and lived at St. Basil Dayara, Pathanamthitta. Catholicos Baselios Augen I honoured him with the title Sabha Kavi, “Poet of the Church”, and Baselios Marthoma Mathews II named him Malankarayude Aprem for his hymns and his translations of liturgical books. He reposed on 4 May 2005 and rests at St. Basil Dayara Chapel.

Son of Zebedee and brother of James, John was the disciple whom Jesus loved, who reclined at the Last Supper, stood by the Cross and received the Virgin Mary into his care. Tradition ascribes to him the Fourth Gospel, three epistles and the Book of Revelation, written in exile on Patmos. He ministered at Ephesus and is said to have lived to a great age, dying there about 100 CE.

The fifth Sunday after Easter draws the Easter season toward the Ascension, when the Lord goes up to the Father. The Church gives thanks for the Resurrection and prepares the faithful to receive the Lord’s parting promise of the Holy Spirit, in whose power the apostles were to be His witnesses to the ends of the earth.

Called the Zealot or the Cananaean, Simon was one of the Twelve and is named in every list of the apostles. Church tradition says that he preached the Gospel in Egypt and in the East, and that he sealed his witness with martyrdom. The Church honours him together with the other apostles who carried the message of Christ to the ends of the earth.

Born Ouseph into the Pallipurath branch of the Pakalomattom family, he was consecrated by the ailing Mar Thoma IV, without any foreign bishop present, and took charge on his death in 1728. He made Kandanad his headquarters and led the Church for thirty-seven years. He reposed on 10 May 1765 and was laid to rest in St. Mary’s Church, Niranam, with Mar Thoma VI conducting the funeral.

Anjilimoottil Itty Thommen Kathanar was the chief adviser and close aide of Archdeacon Thomas, the future Mar Thoma I, in resisting the Portuguese persecutions of the seventeenth century. When the Portuguese imprisoned Ahatallah, he led the twenty-five thousand faithful gathered at Mattancherry, and at his direction they tied a rope to the ancient stone cross and swore never to accept the Roman faith. He convened the Alangad assembly, shared Mar Thoma I’s trials, reposed on 10 May 1659 and was buried at St. Mary’s Church, Kallisserry, where he was vicar.

Cheriamadathil Skariah Malpan was an influential priest, theologian, educator and scholar of the Church, one of the chief Malpans of the Orthodox Theological Seminary, Kottayam, and its principal from 1943 to 1947. He played an important part in the theological education and spiritual formation of the clergy. Elected to the episcopate in 1930, he declined the office. He also wrote Kumbasara Sahayi (Help to Confession), published in 1933, and Yarusalem Yathra (Jerusalem Pilgrimage), published in 1935.

Suloqo, the Ascension, commemorates the fortieth day after the Resurrection, when the risen Lord led His disciples out to the Mount of Olives, blessed them and was taken up into heaven in their sight (Acts 1:1–11; Luke 24:50–53). The Church confesses that He sits at the right hand of the Father, and awaits His coming again in glory.

From the day after the Ascension until the eve of Pentecost, the Malankara Church keeps nine days of preparation, remembering how the apostles waited in prayer in the upper room for the promised gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:12–14). The faithful devote these days to prayer, repentance and readiness, asking that the Spirit may come upon them also.

On 15 May the Church keeps the Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary for good crops and the harvest, asking the intercession of the Mother of God for the fruitful ripening of the fields and for the work of those who till the land. The faithful give thanks to God for the bounty of the earth, as the Church asked for the seed in January.

Born about 613 in Beth Qatraye on the Gulf coast, Isaac, known as Isaac the Syrian or Isaac of Nineveh, became a monk and was consecrated Bishop of Nineveh about 676, but resigned after some five months because the duties of a bishop hindered his life of prayer. Withdrawing into solitude, he wrote the Ascetical Homilies on stillness, repentance and divine love, treasured in the Syriac tradition, and lost his sight through his labours in the Scriptures. He reposed about 700.

Born on 14 January 1920 at Thrikothamangalam, Puthuppally, Yuhanon studied Syriac and theology under Augen Mar Timotheos, learned the monastic life at Pampady Dayara, and was ordained deacon in April 1943 and priest that July. After years as a Malpan of the Seminary he became Ramban in February 1966 and was consecrated Metropolitan at Kolenchery on 24 August 1966, shepherding the Cochin Diocese. He reposed on 16 May 1990 and rests at Sion Seminary, Koratty.

The Sunday before Pentecost falls between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the Church, like the apostles in the upper room, waits in prayer for the Holy Spirit. The faithful are called to be of one mind in prayer, to remember the Lord’s promise of the Comforter, and to prepare to receive the Spirit who will lead them into all truth.

On the Sunday before Pentecost the Church keeps Sunday School Day, praying for the children who are taught the faith in its Sunday Schools and for their teachers. The Sunday School movement in Malankara was pioneered by Sleeba Mar Osthathios, and the Church gives thanks for it and asks that its children may grow in the knowledge and love of Christ.

Born Kurien in 1785 into the Punnathra family of Kottayam, he took part in the meetings that founded the Syrian Seminary. Chosen to succeed Mar Dionysius II, he was ordained bishop by Geevarghese Mar Philoxenos of Thozhiyur on 19 October 1817 and became the eleventh Malankara Metropolitan, enjoying cordial relations with the rulers of Travancore and Cochin. He reposed during an epidemic on 19 May 1825 and was interred in the sanctuary of Kottayam Cheriapally.

Constantine the Great (c. 272–337), proclaimed emperor in 306 and victorious at the Milvian Bridge in 312, ended the persecution of Christians and convened the Council of Nicaea in 325. His mother Helena, a devout Christian, travelled to Jerusalem in her old age and, according to tradition, found the Cross of Christ and built churches at the holy places. The Church honours them as pious rulers who favoured the faith.

The Church commemorates the four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, who wrote the Gospels, together with the Fathers of the three Ecumenical Synods: the 318 of Nicaea in 325, who confessed the divinity of the Son; the 150 of Constantinople in 381, who confessed the Holy Spirit; and the 200 of Ephesus in 431, who confessed Mary as Mother of God.

Pentecost, on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection, commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in the upper room in tongues of fire, and the birth of the Church as they began to preach the Gospel to every nation (Acts 2). The faithful give thanks for the gift of the Spirit and, in the evening, offer the special kneeling prayers of the feast.

Aaron the Illustrious was a Christian monk of Mesopotamia in the fourth century, who came from Serugh in Osrhoene and was a disciple of St. Eugenius (Mar Augen). He built two monasteries near Melitene in Armenia. The Syriac and Malankara Churches keep his feast on Pentecost Monday each year.

Born on 29 October 1921 to Ittyavira Thomas and Sosamma, he trained under Thoma Mar Dionysius and Baselios Augen I, was ordained deacon on 22 May 1947 and priest on 25 January 1950, and worked as a headmaster and mathematics teacher. Consecrated Thomas Mar Timotheos at Kolenchery on 24 August 1966, he was elected successor in 1992 and served as seventh Catholicos of the East from 2005 to 2010. He reposed on 26 May 2014 at Parumala and rests at Mount Tabor Dayara, Pathanapuram.

The first Friday after Pentecost, called Golden Friday, commemorates the healing of the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple by Peter and John, the first miracle of the apostles after Pentecost (Acts 3:1–10). Peter’s words, “Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have I give you”, are remembered as the Church’s true treasure.

Geevarghese Mar Coorilos, the younger brother and successor of Abraham Mar Coorilos, was known as Kattumangat Ilaya Bava or Cheriya Bava and was famed for his piety and prayer. After leading the Thozhiyur community for some years, he reposed on 29 May 1809 and was laid to rest at the Monastery of St. Thomas, Vettikkal, where his tomb became a place of pilgrimage.

The first Sunday after Pentecost opens the long season in which the Church, filled with the Holy Spirit, lives and proclaims the Gospel. The faithful give thanks for the gift of the Spirit and for the apostles through whom the Good News went out to the nations, and ask that the Spirit may guide them in all their ways.

The Synod of Chengannur was held in 1686 at St. Mary’s Old Syrian Church, Chengannur, under Mar Ivanios Hidayatulla, the Antiochene Metropolitan who remained in Malankara after the death of St. Basil Yeldho. The clergy and lay leaders of the Church gathered to order its life and the training of its priests in Syriac and the canons, in the years after the Coonan Cross Oath.

World Environment Day, observed each year on 5 June, was established by the United Nations in 1972 and has been marked since 1974 as a call to care for the natural world. The Church, which gives thanks to God for creation in its worship, uses the day to remind the faithful of their duty to protect the earth and its creatures as stewards of God’s gift.

Born in 1858 into the Karottuveettil family of Kandanad, the son of Korah, he studied Syriac and canon law under Konat Geevarghese Mar Julius and was also a Sanskrit scholar. Consecrated Metropolitan Yuyakim Mar Ivanios by Patriarch Abded Mshiho II at Chengannur on 9 February 1913, he served Kandanad, lived much at Parumala in works of charity and laid the foundation of Pampady Dayara church in 1920. He reposed on 6 June 1925 and rests beside St. Gregorios of Parumala.

Born on 1 July 1955 at Mukkalumon, Ranni, Zachariah Perangattu was ordained deacon in 1979 and priest in 1980 by Catholicos Baselios Marthoma Mathews I. He edited devotional meditations, prayer books and liturgical studies, and was elevated Metropolitan on 5 March 2005. A life of prayer and service to the poor, it ended in an accident on 6 June 2007, while he was on his way to distribute books to poor students. He rests at Vallikkattu Dayara, Vakathanam.

The second Sunday after Pentecost continues the season in which the Church lives by the Holy Spirit and bears witness to the Gospel. The faithful hear the Lord’s call to faith, repentance and the service of others, and are strengthened to follow the apostles’ example in their own homes and places of work.

Bartholomew, generally identified with Nathanael of Cana whom Philip brought to Jesus, is named among the Twelve. Ancient tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says that he preached in India, where Pantaenus later found a Hebrew copy of St. Matthew’s Gospel left by him, and in Arabia, and that he was martyred in Armenia. His memory is cherished in India.

A prelate from Antioch, Shemvun Mar Athanasios came to Malankara after the Synod of Mulanthuruthy in 1876 as a delegate of the Patriarch. He lived at Kottayam Mar Barsauma Orthodox Church, where he taught the clergy and faithful the doctrine of the Church, and later moved to the Seminary to teach there. His health failed within a few months and he reposed on 11 June 1889, being interred on the north side of the altar of Kottayam Mar Barsauma Orthodox Church.

Susanna came from Puthiyacavu in Mavelikkara and became the first Mother Superior of Mount Tabor Convent at Pathanapuram, the largest convent in the Malankara Church, which arose from the vision of Fr. C. M. Thomas, later Thoma Mar Dionysius. She was closely associated with the Shunoyo spiritual fellowship, which first introduced the habit and rule of life for the sisters of the Order of the Sacred Transfiguration.

The third Sunday after Pentecost belongs to the weeks in which the Church recalls the apostles’ mission to the world. The faithful are invited to remember the Lord’s sending of His disciples, to take up their own share in His work, and to pray for the Church’s missionaries and for those who have not yet heard the Gospel.

On 15 June the Church commemorates the founding of the first church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, a witness to the honour that the Church gave to the Mother of God from its earliest days. The faithful give thanks for her intercession and for the churches built in her name, among them many of the oldest churches of Malankara.

The Apostles’ Fast begins on 16 June and lasts thirteen days, until the Feast of Sts. Peter and Paul on 29 June, in honour of the apostles who fasted and prayed after Pentecost before going out to preach the Gospel. The faithful abstain from meat and keep the days with prayer and almsgiving, asking God to strengthen the Church’s witness.

Known as James the Just and called the Lord’s brother, James became the first Bishop of Jerusalem and presided at the council of the apostles recorded in Acts 15. He is the traditional author of the Epistle of James, and the Liturgy of St. James, the ancient rite of Jerusalem, is attributed to him and is still celebrated in the Syriac tradition. He was martyred at Jerusalem about 62 CE.

The fourth Sunday after Pentecost falls in the season of the apostles, when the Church prepares itself, by fasting, for the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul. The faithful are called to remember the cost of the apostles’ witness, to hold fast to the faith they handed on and to live it in love.

Born in the hill country of Judea to the aged Zechariah and Elizabeth, John’s birth was announced by the angel Gabriel to his father in the Temple, who was struck dumb for his doubt. At the child’s naming on the eighth day Zechariah’s tongue was loosed and he sang the Benedictus, prophesying that his son would go before the Lord to prepare His ways. The Church celebrates his nativity as the dawn of the Gospel.

The fifth Sunday after Pentecost is kept near the end of the Apostles’ Fast, when the Church recalls the labours of Peter and Paul and of all the apostles. The faithful are reminded that the Gospel was carried to every land by those who gave up everything for Christ, and are called to be faithful in their own vocation.

The thirteen-day Apostles’ Fast ends on the Feast of St. Peter and St. Paul, when the Church breaks the fast and gives thanks to God for the apostles whose preaching founded the Church. The faithful rejoice in the gift of the Gospel and ask that they may, like the apostles, bear its light to those around them.

St. Peter, the Galilean fisherman Simon, was the first to confess Jesus as the Christ and became the leader of the apostles, teaching at Antioch according to Syriac tradition before going to Rome. St. Paul, formerly the persecutor Saul of Tarsus, was converted on the road to Damascus and became the Apostle of the Gentiles, writing many epistles. According to tradition both were martyred at Rome under Nero in the 60s.

The Church remembers the twelve disciples whom Jesus chose to be with Him and sent out to preach: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Matthias, who was chosen to replace Judas. After Pentecost they carried the Gospel to Judea and to the ends of the earth, and nearly all sealed their witness with martyrdom.

The Synod of Mulanthuruthy was held in 1876 at St. Thomas Church, Mulanthuruthy, under Patriarch Ignatius Peter III, with the Malankara Metropolitan Mar Dionysius V. It gave the Church its administrative order, and in the following months the Patriarch consecrated six metropolitans, among them Gregorios of Parumala. It is remembered as a landmark in the organisation of the Church.

Thomas, one of the Twelve and called Didymus, confessed the risen Lord with the words “My Lord and my God”. The Church of India holds that he landed at Muziris in 52 CE, preached in Malabar and founded the seven churches of Malankara. The Dukhrono of 3 July recalls the translation of his relics from India to Edessa, and the Church reveres him as its father in faith and the apostle of India.

The sixth Sunday after Pentecost follows the Feast of Sts. Peter and Paul and the end of the Apostles’ Fast, and continues the season in which the Church bears witness to the Gospel in the power of the Spirit. The faithful give thanks for the apostles’ preaching and are called to take their own share in the Church’s mission.

Besides the Twelve, the Lord appointed seventy-two disciples (Luke 10:1) and sent them two by two before His face into every town where He Himself was about to come, with the message that the Kingdom of God had drawn near. The Syriac tradition honours them as the evangelists who carried the Gospel through Syria and Mesopotamia and beyond, among them Addai, who preached at Edessa. The Church remembers them with thanksgiving for the mission of the Gospel.

On Mission Sunday the Church prays for and supports its mission work, the proclamation of the Gospel in India and beyond, remembering the Lord’s command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). The faithful give thanks for the missionaries and for the Church’s Mission Board, and are reminded that every baptised person shares in the task of making Christ known.

Mathen Kathanar of the Pakalomattom family was consecrated by Mar Thoma VI at Chengannur on 5 May 1796 and succeeded him as Malankara Metropolitan in April 1808. In December 1808 he placed the Church’s fixed deposit of 3,000 poovarahan, the Vattipanam, with the Travancore government. Bedridden at Kandanad, he consecrated Thoma Kathanar as his successor, reposed on 4 July 1809 and rests at St. Peter’s and St. Paul’s Church, Kolenchery.

Born on 6 August 1924 at Kundara, Zachariah joined Mount Tabor Dayara, Pathanapuram, at fifteen, was ordained deacon in 1945 and priest in 1951, and became a Ramban in 1971. Consecrated Metropolitan in 1978, he led the Madras Diocese from 1979 and founded the Madras Medical Mission. A strict ascetic who translated the Holy Qurbana into Tamil, he reposed on 7 July 1997 and rests at Pathanapuram Dayara.

Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher who became a Christian, headed the catechetical school of Alexandria about 180 CE and was the teacher of Clement of Alexandria. According to Eusebius he travelled to India to preach, where he found Christians who possessed St. Matthew’s Gospel in Hebrew letters, left by the apostle Bartholomew. On his return he resumed his teaching and wrote commentaries on the Scriptures, and he reposed about 200 CE.

Born in 1695 at Karakosh near Mosul, the son of the priest Isahak, Yuhanon and his brother Sleeba were monks at Mor Behnam Monastery, and in 1747 Patriarch George III consecrated him bishop with the title Gregorios. He came to Malankara in the mid-eighteenth century with Maphrian Shukrallah and with Mar Ivanios Yuhanon consecrated Mar Thoma VI as Mar Dionysius I in 1770. Failing in sight in his last years, he reposed on 10 July 1773 and is entombed at Mar Thoman Church, Mulanthuruthy.

Born Kurien into the Kattumangat family, he became a Ramban and nursed the ailing Mar Gregorios Yuhanon in his last years. Ordained Metropolitan Abraham Mar Coorilos in 1772 by the Antiochene bishop Mar Gregorios, he became the first Metropolitan at Thozhiyur and held that charge for thirty years, remembered as Kattumangat Valiya Bava. He reposed on 10 July 1802 and rests at St. George’s Church, Thozhiyur.

Born on 12 November 1833 into the Pulikkottil family of Kunnamkulam, Joseph was ordained priest in 1852 and consecrated Metropolitan Joseph Mar Dionysius by Patriarch Jacob II at Amid on 7 May 1865. As Malankara Metropolitan until 1909 he hosted Patriarch Peter III at the Synod of Mulanthuruthy in 1876, which organised the Church’s administration, and is remembered as Malankara Sabha Thejus. He reposed on 11 July 1909 and was interred on the north side of the Old Seminary Chapel, Kottayam.

The seventh Sunday after Pentecost belongs to the summer weeks of the Church’s year, when the faithful hear the Lord’s teaching and are called to bring forth the fruit of the Spirit. The Church prays for steadfastness in faith and for the grace to live the Gospel in the ordinary tasks of daily life.

Born on 30 August 1946 at Mangad near Kunnamkulam and baptised at St. Mary’s Church, Pazhanji, Paul studied at the Orthodox Theological Seminary, Kottayam, and was ordained deacon in 1973 and priest on 2 June 1973 by Yuhanon Mar Severios. Consecrated Paulose Mar Milithios on 15 May 1985, he became first Metropolitan of Kunnamkulam and, in 2010, eighth Catholicos of the East and Malankara Metropolitan. He reposed on 12 July 2021, aged 74.

Kuriakose was a child of three when his mother Yulithi (Julitta), who had fled persecution, was brought with him before the governor at Tarsus about 304 CE. When the boy cried out that he was a Christian he was dashed to the ground and killed, and his mother, giving thanks to God, was tortured and beheaded. With them the Church honours Mar Abhai of Nicea, an ascetic of Raksan near Mardin who founded the Monastery of Ladders and served as bishop for thirty-two years.

Born about 1890 into the Koottungal family, Very Rev. K. V. Geevarghese Ramban lived a life of prayer and silence that drew many seekers and was known as Thiruvithamcode Rambachan. In 1941 Catholicos Baselios Geevarghese II appointed him Vicar and Manager of St. Mary’s Orthodox Church, Thiruvithamcode, which he renovated and served to the end of his life, and he founded St. Thomas Orthodox Church, Kulasekharam. He reposed on 16 July 1970, aged 80.

These three priests were historical servants of the Thiruvithamcode community in Kanyakumari. As that community gradually died out, the memory of its Kathanars faded, and little is now known of them beyond their names. The Church remembers them together, giving thanks for the faithful shepherds who tended a congregation that has all but disappeared.

The eighth Sunday after Pentecost continues the long season of the Spirit, in which the Church learns from the Gospel to trust in God’s care and to serve the neighbour. The faithful are invited to renew their prayer and almsgiving, and to look forward to the fast and feast of the Mother of God that lie ahead.

From the Malikayil family of Pathamuttom, he was a prominent priest who served as the first vicar of Pathamuttom Sleeba Church and in 1943 founded St. Mary’s Chapel at Pathamuttom as a monastic chapel. He was also the first chief editor of *Malankara Sabha*, the official magazine of the Malankara Church, established in 1946 under Catholicos Baselios Geevarghese II, and wrote several Malayalam liturgical and devotional works, including *Prarthana Yogamithram* and *Ettu Nombil*.

Elijah the Tishbite, prophet of Israel in the days of King Ahab, called the nation back to the Lord and confronted the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, where fire fell from heaven on his sacrifice. Fed by ravens, he fled to Horeb, heard the Lord in a still small voice, and was taken up in a whirlwind in a chariot of fire. He appeared with Moses at the Transfiguration and is honoured as a model of zeal and prayer.

Mary of Magdala, whom Jesus healed of seven demons, became a faithful follower who stood at the foot of the Cross, watched the burial and came to the tomb at dawn with spices. She was the first to see the risen Lord, who sent her to tell the apostles, and the Church therefore calls her the apostle to the apostles and a myrrh-bearer. Tradition says she later lived at Ephesus and was laid to rest there.

A nineteenth-century priest, Syriac scholar and Malpan, Geevarghese Ramban belonged to a family of Arthat–Kunnamkulam origin that fled Tipu Sultan’s invasion and settled at Thrippunithura. Born on 22 Medam 1829, he was made deacon by Cheppad Mar Dionysius in 1840 and ordained priest at Nadamel Church in 1851. Patriarch Ignatius Peter III later raised him to Ramban at Mulanthuruthy, and Pulikkottil Joseph Mar Dionysius II appointed him Malpan at the Old Seminary, Kottayam.

Born on 12 October 1926 at Kozhencherry, the youngest son of Kunjupappi and Achamma of the Thevervelil family, Geevarghese studied at the Madurai American College and Madras Christian College and took a master’s degree in Sociology. Consecrated Metropolitan in 1978, he led the Thiruvananthapuram Diocese and in 1991 founded its Charitable and Educational Society to establish institutions of higher education. He reposed on 23 July 1999 and rests at Holy Trinity Ashram, Ranny.

Born on 20 October 1850 at Anjediva, Goa, the youngest son of Custodio Santa Anna de Noronha, Roque Zephrin Noronha was ordained priest in Goa and, troubled by the injustice there, joined Alvares Mar Julius in his mission along the west coast from Mangalore to Bombay. When Alvares was consecrated bishop, St. Mary’s Church, Brahmavar, was entrusted to him, and he became its first Vicar General. He reposed on 23 July 1936 and was declared a regional saint on 6 December 2015.

Born in Palestine about 310, Epiphanius lived as a monk and founded a monastery before becoming Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus in 367. A zealous defender of the Nicene faith, he wrote the Panarion against eighty heresies and opposed the teachings of Origen, and was honoured for his charity and asceticism. He reposed at sea in 403 while returning from Constantinople to his island.

The ninth Sunday after Pentecost is one of the last Sundays of the season of the apostles’ mission, when the Church hears again the Lord’s call to watchfulness and faith. The faithful pray that the Holy Spirit may keep them steadfast, and prepare to keep the Fast of the Assumption of St. Mary.

Born about 390 at Sisan on the border of Syria and Cilicia, Simeon became a monk and then settled on a pillar near Aleppo, where he lived for some thirty-seven years in prayer and fasting, guiding the crowds who came to him and writing to emperors and bishops. His endurance made him a great spiritual father of Syria, imitated by many pillar-saints after him. He reposed in 459 CE.

Born in 1226 at Melitene, the son of the physician Aaron, Gregory Bar Ebraya studied medicine and philosophy at Antioch and Tripoli, was consecrated bishop at the age of twenty and became Maphrian of the East in 1264. A scholar of extraordinary range, he wrote on theology, philosophy, science, history, law and grammar, among them the Ethicon, the Book of Rays and the Nomocanon. He reposed at Maragha in 1286 and rests at Mar Mattai Monastery near Mosul.

The fifteen-day fast of the Assumption begins on 1 August and prepares the faithful for the Feast of the Departure of the Mother of God on 15 August. The faithful abstain from meat and keep the days with prayer and almsgiving, asking the intercession of the Virgin Mary, who prayed and fasted in faithfulness to the Lord all her life.

Shmuni, a Jewish mother, and her seven sons were seized under the king Antiochus IV Epiphanes about 167 BCE and commanded to eat swine’s flesh against the Law. The aged scribe Eliazar, their teacher, refused first, and the seven brothers were tortured to death one by one, each confessing faith in the resurrection, while their mother encouraged them before dying herself. The Church honours these Maccabean martyrs as forerunners of the Christian martyrs.

Born on 26 January 1946 at Kurichy, the second child of K. K. John and Mariamma, he studied physics at S. B. College, Changanassery, joined Bethany Ashram in 1968 and was ordained priest in 1974. After theological studies at Bishop’s College, Calcutta, and Leeds, he served as superior of Bethany Ashram, became Ramban in 1992 and was consecrated bishop in 1993, becoming first Metropolitan of the Mavelikara Diocese. He reposed on 1 August 2012 and rests at Bethany Ashram, Perunad.

The eleventh Sunday after Pentecost, which falls only in years when Easter comes early, is one of the last Sundays of the season after Pentecost, before the Feast of the Transfiguration. The Church gives thanks for the Spirit’s gifts through the summer weeks and prays that the faithful may continue in faith as the great feasts of the Lord and His Mother draw near.

The tenth Sunday after Pentecost falls in the days of the Fast of the Assumption, when the Church turns toward the Mother of God and the Lord’s Transfiguration. The faithful are called to strengthen their prayer and repentance, and to listen to the Gospel of the Lord, who sustains His people through the fast.

The Transfiguration commemorates the day on which Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and His face shone like the sun and His garments became white as light, while Moses and Elijah spoke with Him and the Father’s voice declared Him the beloved Son (Matthew 17:1–9). The feast, called Koodara, shows the glory of the Lord that awaits the faithful in the Kingdom.

Born on 28 August 1888 at Niranam as M. M. Alexander, son of Mathai and Kunjamma of Mattackal, he was ordained deacon in 1907 and priest in 1918, the year he helped found Bethany Ashram at Perunad. Consecrated Metropolitan by Catholicos Baselios Geevarghese II on 7 April 1938 for Kollam and the Church’s dioceses outside Kerala, he remained closely bound to Bethany until his repose on 6 August 1965. He rests at St. John’s Chapel, Bethany Ashram, Perunad.

Demetrius, a young Roman officer and Christian of Thessalonica, was imprisoned under the emperor Maximian about 306 CE for preaching Christ and was pierced with spears. His courage inspired his friend Nestor, who overcame the gladiator Lyaeus in the arena, and his tomb became a great shrine to which the people of Thessalonica looked as their protector. The Church honours him as a martyr.

Born between about 1770 and 1780 into the Marunthalizhikathu family of Anchal, Younan Kathanar was regarded as a saint by his neighbours in his lifetime. He walked the sixteen kilometres between Anchal and Kottarakkara Church to serve as priest and later made his home in the church compound. He told the people to open his grave on the forty-first day after his death, and they found his body largely incorrupt. He reposed on 22 Karkidakam and rests within the altar of Kottarakkara Church; St. George’s, Anchal, keeps his memory.

The first Sunday after the Transfiguration invites the faithful to remember the glory of Christ shown to the apostles on the mountain, and to carry the memory of it down into the valley of daily life. The Church prays that, as the disciples listened to the Beloved Son, so the faithful may hear and follow Him.

Rabban Ramban was one of the three monks who came to Malankara in 905 CE with the prelate Mar Danaha, the others being Yaunan Ramban and Avan, who is thought to be Mar Abo. They were sent from the East by Mor Athanasius, the Maphrian, consecrated that year by Patriarch Dionysius II of Antioch. Rabban Ramban reposed on 24 Karkidakam 905 CE at the house of Kuruvila of the Nadayil family at Chennithala and was laid to rest in a plot of land near that house.

A Roman citizen born at Samosata or in Phrygia, the boy Azazael came to Rome with his uncle and lived on the Caelian hill. When he was only fourteen he was ordered to be put to death for confessing Christ, and was beheaded in 304 CE, receiving the martyr’s crown. He is known in the West as St. Pancras, and the Church of Mor Azazael at Keferze in Tur Abdin is dedicated to him.

Geevarghese Kathanar of the Neduvampurathu family was a priest who was killed by local Hindus at Kaippattoor, and the Church remembers him as a martyr. On his feast day each year the members of the Neduvampurathu Kudumbayogam hold special prayers at the Kaippattoor Church.

Micah of Moresheth, a prophet in Judah in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, spoke against the injustice of the rich and the deceit of false prophets, and called the people to do justice, love mercy and walk humbly with God. His book foretells the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem and the birth of a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, a prophecy the Church sees fulfilled in Christ.

Shunoyo, the Feast of the Assumption, commemorates the falling asleep of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, whom the apostles gathered to bury in Jerusalem, and the taking up of her body to heaven, according to the Church’s tradition. The Church honours her as the Mother of the Lord and the first of the redeemed, and keeps the feast after a fast of fifteen days.

The fifteen-day fast of the Assumption ends on the Feast of the Assumption of St. Mary, when the Church breaks the fast with the Holy Qurbana and gives thanks for the Mother of God. The faithful rejoice in the Virgin’s departure to her Son and ask her prayers, and return to their ordinary food with thanksgiving.

Born on 17 January 1854, Abded Mshiho became a monk in 1873, priest in 1875 and bishop in 1886, and was enthroned Patriarch of Antioch in 1895. Deposed in 1903, he accepted Vattasseril Mar Dionysius’s invitation and reached Kerala on 13 June 1912. On 15 September 1912 he consecrated Mar Ivanios as Baselios Paulose I at Niranam and issued the bulls re-establishing the Catholicate of the East in Malankara. He reposed on 30 August 1915 at Mor Hananyo Monastery, Mardin.

The Martha Mariam Samajam is the women’s association of the Church, named after the Blessed Virgin Mary, and works for the spiritual life of women and for charity and service in the parishes. It keeps its day on the Feast of the Assumption of St. Mary, when its members pray and give thanks for the Mother of God, whom they take as their patron and model.

The chapel of the Catholicate Palace at Devalokam, Kottayam, the seat of the Catholicos of the East, keeps its annual feast on 15 August, the Feast of the Assumption of St. Mary. The Catholicate Aramana, raised in the time of Baselios Geevarghese II, is the headquarters of the Church’s Catholicos, and the feast is kept with prayer and the Holy Qurbana.

On 15 August 1947 India became independent after a long struggle for freedom. The Church gives thanks for the freedom of the nation and for those who worked and suffered for it, and prays for the leaders and people of India, that the country may be guided by justice, peace and care for the poor.

The second Sunday after the Transfiguration, which falls only in some years, continues the Church’s reflection on the glory of Christ shown on the mountain. The faithful are reminded that the glory seen by the apostles is the glory to which the Lord calls His people, and are urged to listen to the Beloved Son in the Scriptures.

The first Sunday after the Feast of the Assumption begins the weeks in which the Church, having honoured the Mother of God at her departure, continues to give thanks for her intercession. The faithful look toward the feast of her birth, and are reminded that her faith and obedience are the pattern of their own.

A native of Karakosh near Mosul, Hidayatulla was consecrated bishop to assist Maphrian Yeldho and travelled with him to Kothamangalam in 1685, where the dying Maphrian raised him to Metropolitan. For eight years he carried on the apostolic work, convened a synod at Chengannur in 1686, trained priests in Syriac and the Church’s canons and consecrated Mar Thoma III and Mar Thoma IV. He reposed on 16 August 1693 and is entombed at Mar Thoman Church, Mulanthuruthy.

Jude, called Thaddaeus and Labbaeus, was one of the Twelve and is remembered for his question to the Lord at the Last Supper, asking why He would show Himself to the disciples and not to the world. Tradition says that he preached the Gospel in Judea, Syria and Mesopotamia and was martyred, and the short Epistle of Jude is attributed to him. The Church honours him among the apostles.

The Church commemorates all the prophets of the Old Covenant, from Moses and Samuel to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel and the Twelve, whom the Holy Spirit sent to call Israel back to the Lord and to foretell the coming of the Messiah. Their writings, read in the services throughout the year, announced the birth of Christ from the Virgin and His Passion and Resurrection, and the Church gives thanks for their witness.

Born on 19 June 1926 at North Mulakulam to Iype Varkey Poovathumkal and Annamma Valiyakattayil, he was made Ramban on 16 February 1975 at Puthenkavu and consecrated Metropolitan by Catholicos Baselios Augen I at Niranam the next day.
